title: 3D trigonometry
examples: How do I find the angle when I have a box?
What is the formula for the angle between a line and a plane?
Can I use vectors for this problem?

explain.say: Today we learn about angles in three dimensions. We will find the angle between a line and a plane.
The angle we find is between the line and the plane itself. We use the concept of projection to help us.
Imagine a line sticking out from a flat surface. The angle is measured by dropping a perpendicular line onto the plane.
We can then use standard 2D trigonometry on the resulting right-angled triangle. Remember sine, cosine, and tangent.
For example, if a line goes up from a base, the angle uses the height and the horizontal distance.

faq.q: What is the angle between a line and a plane?
faq.a: It is the angle formed between the line and its projection onto the plane. Think of it like the steepest angle you can make on that surface.
asks: How do I measure this angle?
What is the angle of inclination to the plane?

faq.q: Do I always need a right-angled triangle?
faq.a: Yes, finding this angle usually requires creating a right-angled triangle involving the perpendicular line. This makes the standard trigonometric ratios work.
asks: Can I use non-right triangles here?

faq.q: What is the projection of a line onto a plane?
faq.a: The projection is the shadow the line casts onto the plane. This shadow forms one side of the right-angled triangle we use for calculation.
asks: How do I find the horizontal distance?

faq.q: Does the angle change if I move the line?
faq.a: The angle depends on the line's direction relative to the plane. If the line becomes parallel to the plane, the angle is zero degrees.
asks: If the line is flat, what is the angle?
What if the line is parallel to the surface?

faq.q: Can I use vectors to solve this?
faq.a: Yes, vector methods are a very powerful way to solve this problem. They provide a systematic way to find the angle between two directional components.
asks: Is there an alternative to trigonometry?

facts: The angle between a line and a plane is measured in degrees.
The angle is determined by the line's steepness relative to the plane.
A perpendicular line segment is crucial for setting up the calculation.
The projection forms the adjacent side in the resulting right triangle.

quiz.say: A ramp rises 3 meters vertically over a horizontal distance of 10 meters. What is the angle the ramp makes with the ground?
quiz.why: The tangent ratio uses the opposite side (height) over the adjacent side (run) to find the angle.

wrong.1: Sine uses the hypotenuse, and we do not know the hypotenuse directly.
wrong.2: Cosine uses the adjacent side over the hypotenuse, and we do not know the hypotenuse.
wrong.3: This is just the ratio, not the angle itself in degrees.

quiz.say: If a ladder leans against a vertical wall, forming a right angle with the ground, and the angle with the ground is 60 degrees, what is the ratio of the height to the ladder length?
quiz.why: Sine relates the opposite side (height) to the hypotenuse (ladder length), giving the required ratio.

wrong.0: This calculation is incorrect and does not represent any standard trigonometric relationship here.
wrong.2: Cosine relates the adjacent side (ground) to the hypotenuse, not the height.
wrong.3: Tangent relates the height to the ground, but we need the height to the total length.

quiz.say: A line segment connects point A (0, 0, 0) to point B (5, 0, 3). What is the angle this line makes with the x-axis (the plane y=0)?
quiz.why: The angle with the x-axis uses the vertical change (3) over the horizontal change (5) in the plane.

wrong.1: Division by zero is undefined, and this setup is for the y-z plane, not the x-axis.
wrong.2: This is the ratio, not the angle in degrees.
wrong.3: Sine would require knowing the actual length of the line segment, which is the hypotenuse.
